doc.title: Chris Parker interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, January 5, 2023

title: Taking direction and being a chameleon
summary: When told not to play something he starts fresh, takes producers' direction and can emulate drummers like Fred White, Purdie, Grady Tate; Rowe relays Purdie's reply.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: Have you ever had someone say to you, “I don’t want you to do that.”?
Yes. And that’s a point of departure, you know and at that moment — somebody said, “You’re very diplomatic.” So my diplomacy kind of kicks in and detente comes to mind

where okay they don’t want me to do what I do naturally or instinctually or what I prepared to do when I first heard about this song or this album. So leave all that behind and start fresh. And I take their direction or the producer’s direction, you know, don’t do this, do this, can you make it sound like this, can you make it go faster, slower, louder, softer. Can you play with brushes? Can you play with — whatever the suggestions might be you take it all in and process it and then go forward with that. You know? So it’s not that I’m changeable but I guess you could say I’m chameleon-like, you know somebody wants it to sound like a lot of times they say I want you to sound like this drummer or that, or I want this kind of feel from this record. Fine. You know I have no problem emulating Fred White, Earth, Wind and Fire, that drummer, great drummer just passed away recently, or Bernard Purdie or Grady Tate is one of my favorites, or Al Jackson or Roger Hawkins.
It’s funny you mentioned Bernard Purdie because he told me if someone said, “I want you to sound like Steve Gadd he would have said, “Well go get Steve Gadd then.”
